title: Fair dealing
hook: pay fairly, charge fairly, keep promises
tomorrow: first full paycheck, and a pay-in-four button. what's enough?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a steel bracelet tapped by a small boy: faith at work, kept on and explained in one breath. Today it's money's turn.

Payday at the stall comes in an envelope. Simran counts it at the bus stop and comes up one hour short: the extra hour she stayed to pack up when it rained. And that same morning, a man paid with a twenty and walked off before she could hand him his change. It's still in her apron pocket. Two mistakes, one against her and one in her favor. Her first thought: well, that's even.
screen: `AN ENVELOPE, ONE HOUR SHORT.` → `A STRANGER'S CHANGE IN HER APRON.` → `SO, EVEN?`

segments.voice: Not even, says the Sikh idea of fair dealing, because it runs in every direction: pay fairly, charge fairly, keep promises. Guru Nanak makes the point with real force, on ang 141, and he does it by borrowing two neighbors' own deepest lines. In paraphrase: to take what rightfully belongs to another is like pork to a Muslim, and like beef to a Hindu. Each listener hears the thing their own tradition most refuses, and the Guru says: that's how someone else's due should look to you. The Punjabi word for that due is hakk, a person's rightful share. So the two mistakes don't cancel. They're two separate hakks. The man's change is his. Simran seals it in an envelope with a note, tapes it inside the cash box, and tells Mrs. Ortega to watch for him next Saturday. And the missing hour? Fair dealing isn't only not taking. It's also asking, plainly, for what was agreed. She texts Mrs. Ortega: i think i'm missing an hour from the rainy Saturday. No accusing, just the fact. Mrs. Ortega writes back within a minute: my mistake, so sorry, I'll fix it this week. Two promises kept, one on each side of the stall. Nobody shaved. Nobody shamed.
screen: `FAIR DEALING RUNS EVERY WAY.` · `ANG 141: ANOTHER'S DUE, LIKE A TABOO.` · `HAKK: A RIGHTFUL SHARE.` · `RETURN IT; ASK PLAINLY.` · then, large: `DEAL FAIRLY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind anything small you owe: a few dollars, a borrowed book, a reply you promised. If you can settle it now, do it: send the money, send the message. If you can't yet, choose the exact time you will, and sit with it settled.
Fair dealing. Paying fairly, charging fairly and keeping promises, so no one's rightful share is taken.
Your line: deal fairly. Nobody shaved and nobody shamed, on either side of the stall. Back tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1664 COUNTS.` → `LIVING IT · 38 OF 134.` → `TOMORROW: A PAY-IN-FOUR BUTTON. WHAT'S ENOUGH?`
